# Executive Summary

<!--
This section provides a condensed view of the entire proposal, one page long.
It should be a comprehensive high-level overview that captures the essence of the proposal, including its goals, methods, expected outcomes, deliverables, and budget.
-->
Clinical prediction models are increasingly evaluated across hospitals, countries and health systems [@riley2016]. However, many institutions cannot transfer patient-level data because of governance, ethical, legal or operational constraints. Existing federated platforms provide important analytical capabilities, but may require dedicated client-server infrastructure or a common data model. Research networks working with heterogeneous local datasets therefore still recreate variable mapping, quality checks, validation code, output review and cross-site reporting for each study.
We propose fedvalidateR, an open-source R package that will convert a multisite external-validation protocol into a reusable, version-controlled workflow. Participating sites will map local data to a shared specification, run standardised checks and analyses in ordinary R, and review a structured aggregate results object before release. Central functions will verify compatibility, compare site-specific performance, quantify heterogeneity and generate reproducible reports. The first release will support existing clinical prediction models for binary outcomes, such as mortality, clinical deterioration and hospital readmission.
The project will deliver an installable R package, documented study and site-results specifications, synthetic multisite datasets, automated tests, tutorials and an end-to-end reproducible demonstration. Evaluation will use fully specified prediction models or risk scores with synthetic and publicly available data partitioned to simulate independent sites. Subject to data-access and governance approvals, the workflow may also be user-tested in Brazilian intensive care settings, building on experience from the SOFA-2 validation study, or within the ISARIC research network. The project requests US$5,500 over 10 months, and the resulting package, documentation and reproducible examples will be made openly available to the R community.
